newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala to begin digging up details of dirty war.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala to begin digging up details of dirty war.

text.p: A high-level commision will start work next month digging up the truth about human rights violations during Guatemala's three-decade "dirty war," one of its three members said on Monday.
After months of delays due to a lack of money, the panel will be installed on July 31 and start work the next day, Alfredo Balsells, a Guatemalan attorney, told Reuters.

It will take testimony from thousands of Guatemalans who witnessed massacres, murders, kidnappings and disappearances during a civil war between leftist rebels and the country's military regimes that ended with a peace accord in December.
Some 140,000 people were killed or "disappeared" during the 36-year conflict.
Balsells, German law professor and human rights expert Christian Tomuschat and Guatemalan professor Otilia Lux were named to the commission in February, but given no funds.
Earlier this month they were pledged about $5 million in international funds at the United Nations.
The money, still $2.5 million short of the commission's $7.5 million target, was given by Canada, the United States, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Holland and Guatemala.
The rest is expected to come from other donors, such as France and Japan, Barsells added.
Although Guatemala received pledges of more than $1 billion in international loans and donations for peacetime development, none of that money was earmarked for the truth commission.
The commission has hired more than 120 investigators, security guards, historians, computer experts and social scientists. It has a year to finish its report.
Balsells said he hopes combatants from both sides of the war as well as civilian victims will testify.
Human rights groups have criticised the commission's mandate, which is to tell the history of the war without naming those who committed the human rights abuses.

But Balsells said the work of the commission would be easier if it did not have to defend itself against charges of slander and defamation by coming up with evidence that would stand up in a court of law.
